priceData.title: Realtor Commission on $500k House: $25,000–$30,000 (2026)
priceData.metaDescription: How much commission on a $500,000 home sale? At 5-6%, agent fees total $25,000-$30,000, leaving $470,000-$475,000 net. Calculate post-NAR settlement savings.
priceData.h1: Realtor Commission on a $500,000 Home Sale
priceData.aeoDirectAnswer: How much commission on a $500,000 home sale? At a typical 5% to 6% total rate, that comes to $25,000 to $30,000 in total agent fees, leaving the seller with estimated net proceeds of $470,000 to $475,000. In a typical 50/50 split, the listing agent and buyer's agent each receive $12,500 to $15,000.
priceData.narContext: The August 2024 NAR settlement removed mandatory buyer-broker compensation from MLS listing databases nationwide. On a $500,000 property—closely aligned with the national median price of single-family homes—sellers can unbundle representation costs, negotiating the listing side independently (e.g., 2.5% or $12,500) and evaluating buyer concessions on a per-offer basis.
priceData.secondaryAngleTitle: Median US Single-Family Price & Step-by-Step Calculation
secondaryAngleContent: The $500,000 price point represents the benchmark transaction in many active US suburban and metropolitan markets. It is also one of the most frequently searched real estate queries, often searched in word-problem phrasing like 'how much does a realtor make on a $500,000 sale?'

The arithmetic is straightforward: multiply the final sale price ($500,000) by the total agreed commission percentage. At 6.0%, $500,000 × 0.06 = $30,000. At 5.0%, $500,000 × 0.05 = $25,000. Every 0.5% reduction in commission rate translates to an exact $2,500 cash difference in the seller's pocket.

In today's market, many sellers negotiate a tiered or discount listing fee of 2.0% ($10,000) while offering 2.5% ($12,500) to the cooperating buyer's broker, bringing the total cost down to 4.5% ($22,500) and putting an extra $7,500 directly into the seller's bank account.

faqs.q: How much does a realtor make on a $500,000 house sale?
faqs.a: At the typical 5% to 6% rate, total broker commissions equal $25,000 to $30,000. Split between both sides, the listing broker and buyer broker each receive $12,500 to $15,000. The individual agent then splits their portion with their sponsoring brokerage according to their split agreement (e.g., 70/30 or 80/20).

faqs.q: What is 6 percent of 500 000 dollars in real estate?
faqs.a: Six percent (6%) of $500,000 is exactly $30,000. Under traditional 50/50 broker splits, this represents $15,000 paid to the seller's listing brokerage and $15,000 paid to the buyer's brokerage.

faqs.q: How much can I save by negotiating commission on a $500k house?
faqs.a: Negotiating from 6.0% down to 4.5% saves you $7,500 ($22,500 total commission vs. $30,000). Negotiating to a 4.0% total fee saves a full $10,000, increasing your net proceeds from $470,000 to $480,000.

otherPrices.title: Realtor Commission on $300k House: $15,000–$18,000 (2026)
otherPrices.metaDescription: How much commission on a $300k home sale? At 5-6%, expect $15,000-$18,000 in agent fees with $282,000-$285,000 net proceeds. Calculate your exact payout.
otherPrices.h1: Realtor Commission on a $300,000 Home Sale
otherPrices.aeoDirectAnswer: How much commission on a $300,000 home sale? At a typical 5% to 6% total rate, that comes to $15,000 to $18,000 in total agent fees, leaving the seller with estimated net proceeds of $282,000 to $285,000. In a typical 50/50 split, the listing agent and buyer's agent each receive $7,500 to $9,000.
otherPrices.narContext: Following the landmark 2024 National Association of Realtors (NAR) settlement, sellers are no longer obligated to offer blanket compensation to buyer's agents on the Multiple Listing Service (MLS). On a $300,000 sale, you have full legal flexibility to negotiate your listing agent's fee (often 2.0% to 2.5%, or $6,000 to $7,500) and decide whether or not to offer a concession toward the buyer's broker fee.
otherPrices.secondaryAngleTitle: First-Time Home Sellers & Starter Home Equity Protection
secondaryAngleContent: At the $300,000 price point—representative of starter homes, suburban condominiums, and entry-level single-family residences—real estate commissions consume a substantially larger proportion of the seller's accumulated net equity than in luxury tiers.

If you purchased your home with a low down payment and currently owe $240,000 on your mortgage, paying a standard 6% commission ($18,000) eats up 30% of your entire $60,000 home equity before accounting for title insurance, transfer taxes, and escrow settlement fees.

However, starter-home sellers must weigh negotiation carefully: many $300,000 buyers are first-time purchasers utilizing FHA, VA, or conventional low-down-payment loans who may lack additional out-of-pocket cash to pay their own buyer's agent. Offering a 2.5% ($7,500) buyer-broker concession can preserve your buyer pool and drive faster, competitive offers without stalling negotiations.

faqs.q: How much does a realtor make on a $300,000 house sale?
faqs.a: At a standard 5% to 6% commission rate, the total commission on a $300,000 home sale is $15,000 to $18,000. If split equally between the listing agent and buyer's agent, each agent's brokerage receives between $7,500 and $9,000 before internal broker-agent splits.

faqs.q: How much does the seller walk away with on a $300k house after commission?
faqs.a: After deducting a 5% to 6% commission ($15,000 to $18,000), the seller receives gross proceeds of $282,000 to $285,000. Your final net payout will also depend on your remaining mortgage payoff balance, transfer taxes, and routine closing fees (typically 1% to 2%).

faqs.q: Can I negotiate a lower commission rate on a $300,000 home?
faqs.a: Yes. Post-NAR settlement rules make all fees strictly negotiable. Negotiating your total commission down to 4.0% saves you $6,000 compared to a traditional 6.0% fee ($12,000 total commission vs. $18,000).

otherPrices.title: Realtor Commission on $750k House: $37,500–$45,000 (2026)
otherPrices.metaDescription: Selling a $750k home? At 5-6% commission, agent fees reach $37,500-$45,000. Calculate net proceeds, dual-agent splits, and post-NAR negotiation savings.
otherPrices.h1: Realtor Commission on a $750,000 Home Sale
otherPrices.aeoDirectAnswer: How much commission on a $750,000 home sale? At a typical 5% to 6% total rate, that comes to $37,500 to $45,000 in total agent fees, leaving the seller with estimated net proceeds of $705,000 to $712,500. In a typical 50/50 split, the listing agent and buyer's agent each receive $18,750 to $22,500.
otherPrices.narContext: In the $750,000 price range, commission dollars grow large enough that traditional percentage fees face heightened competition. Under post-NAR rules requiring written buyer representation agreements, buyers are acutely aware of broker compensation, giving $750k sellers greater leverage to negotiate customized compensation structures.
secondaryAngleContent: At $750,000—common for move-up family homes in competitive suburban enclaves—a 6% commission reaches a significant $45,000. Because the broker's workload to market a $750,000 home is rarely double that of a $375,000 home, sellers possess substantial negotiating leverage.

A primary strategy in this bracket is dual-transaction representation: if you hire the same real estate agent to sell your existing $750,000 home and purchase your next property, agents will frequently discount their listing commission to 1.5% or 2.0% ($11,250 to $15,000) in exchange for the guaranteed purchase business.
Pairing a 2.0% listing fee with a 2.5% buyer-broker concession reduces your total commission outlay to 4.5% ($33,750)—saving you $11,250 in cash compared to an unnegotiated 6.0% standard.

faqs.q: How much commission do realtors make on a $750,000 home?
faqs.a: At 5% to 6%, total commission ranges from $37,500 to $45,000. Under an equal split, the listing agent's office and buyer agent's office each receive $18,750 to $22,500.

faqs.q: What are the net proceeds from selling a $750k house?
faqs.a: After deducting 5% to 6% in real estate agent commissions, your net proceeds from the sale are between $705,000 and $712,500. Routine transfer taxes, title fees, and mortgage payoff will be subtracted from this remaining balance.

faqs.q: Can I use a 1% listing agent on a $750,000 house?
faqs.a: Yes. Many full-service discount brokerages offer 1.0% to 1.5% listing fees ($7,500 to $11,250). If you pair a 1.5% listing fee with a 2.5% buyer concession, your total commission is 4.0% ($30,000), saving you $15,000 compared to a 6% fee.

otherPrices.title: Realtor Commission on $1 Million House (2026 Calculator)
otherPrices.metaDescription: How much commission on a $1M home sale? At 4.5-5.5%, fees equal $45,000-$55,000. Calculate luxury negotiation savings, capped rates, and net proceeds.
otherPrices.h1: Realtor Commission on a $1,000,000 Home Sale
otherPrices.aeoDirectAnswer: How much commission on a $1,000,000 home sale? At typical luxury rates of 4.5% to 5.5%, total agent commission ranges from $45,000 to $55,000, providing net proceeds to the seller of $945,000 to $955,000. At the traditional 6% standard, total commission would reach $60,000 ($30,000 per side).
otherPrices.narContext: In the 7-figure luxury real estate tier, the August 2024 NAR settlement has accelerated the decline of rigid 6% commission models. Luxury buyers routinely negotiate private representation agreements with flat fees or tiered retainers, giving $1M sellers tremendous freedom to negotiate customized compensation packages.
otherPrices.secondaryAngleTitle: Luxury Market Dynamics & High-Value Fee Negotiation Norms
secondaryAngleContent: In the $1,000,000+ luxury tier, paying an unnegotiated 6% commission ($60,000) is increasingly uncommon. Because high-value properties generate substantial commission dollars for brokerages, sophisticated sellers treat commission as an open business negotiation rather than a fixed transaction tax.

Common negotiation norms in 7-figure sales include tiered performance incentives (e.g., 4% on the first $900,000 and 8% on every dollar achieved above $1,000,000), flat-rate listing fees ($15,000 to $20,000) plus marketing costs, or capped maximum broker compensation.
Even a modest reduction from 6.0% down to 4.5% preserves $15,000 in liquid equity, while negotiating down to 4.0% ($40,000 total) keeps an extra $20,000 of your wealth intact.

faqs.q: How much does a realtor make on a $1 million dollar house?
faqs.a: At a 5% to 6% rate, total commission is $50,000 to $60,000. In competitive luxury markets where 4.5% to 5.0% is negotiated, total fees average $45,000 to $50,000, with $22,500 to $25,000 allocated to each brokerage side.

faqs.q: Do luxury home sellers pay lower commission percentages?
faqs.a: Yes. Due to the high dollar volume, luxury sellers frequently negotiate lower percentage rates (4.0% to 5.0%) or structured tiered compensation. A 1% difference on a $1 million sale equals $10,000 in net seller savings.

faqs.q: What will I net from selling a $1,000,000 home?
faqs.a: After deducting typical real estate commissions (4.5% to 5.5%, or $45,000 to $55,000), you will receive gross net proceeds between $945,000 and $955,000 before subtracting your existing mortgage payoff, state transfer taxes, and escrow closing costs.
